Chemical Reactions and Equations.question: Which of the following observations confirms that a chemical reaction has definitely taken place?
options: Evolution of a new gas with distinct chemical properties
Only change in the physical state of matter
Chemical Reactions and Equations.correctAnswer: Evolution of a new gas with distinct chemical properties
Chemical Reactions and Equations.explanation: Evolution of a new chemically distinct gas or formation of a precipitate indicates bond breaking and forming, whereas melting or dissolution are physical changes.

Chemical Reactions and Equations.question: In the reaction: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, which substance is oxidized?
Chemical Reactions and Equations.explanation: Hydrogen gains oxygen to form H₂O, which means H₂ is oxidized. CuO loses oxygen and is reduced to Cu.

Chemical Reactions and Equations.question: Why is respiration considered an exothermic reaction?
options: Glucose oxidizes to release energy in the form of ATP and heat
It absorbs solar energy to break chemical bonds
It requires heat from the surroundings to proceed
No energy transformation occurs during respiration
Chemical Reactions and Equations.correctAnswer: Glucose oxidizes to release energy in the form of ATP and heat
Chemical Reactions and Equations.explanation: Respiration is the cellular combustion/oxidation of glucose producing CO₂, H₂O, and releasing substantial heat/ATP energy.

Chemical Reactions and Equations.question: What is observed when quicklime (CaO) is added to water?
options: A vigorous reaction occurs releasing a large amount of heat to form slaked lime
The container cools down due to endothermic absorption
A clear blue solution forms without any heat change
Hydrogen gas bubbles evolve with a pop sound
Chemical Reactions and Equations.correctAnswer: A vigorous reaction occurs releasing a large amount of heat to form slaked lime
Chemical Reactions and Equations.explanation: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + Heat. It is an intense combination reaction that releases significant thermal energy.

Chemical Reactions and Equations.question: What type of reaction occurs when silver chloride (AgCl) turns grey in sunlight?
Chemical Reactions and Equations.explanation: Sunlight breaks down white AgCl into grey elemental silver (Ag) and chlorine gas (Cl₂): 2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂.

Chemical Reactions and Equations.question: Why do iron nails turn brown and copper sulphate solution fade from blue to light green when nails are dipped in it?
options: Iron displaces copper from CuSO₄ because iron is more reactive
Copper oxidizes iron to form iron oxide
It is a neutralisation reaction forming a salt
Iron nail absorbs the blue pigment of copper sulphate
Chemical Reactions and Equations.correctAnswer: Iron displaces copper from CuSO₄ because iron is more reactive
Chemical Reactions and Equations.explanation: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu. Fe is above Cu in the activity series, so it displaces Cu, forming green FeSO₄ and reddish-brown Cu deposit.

Chemical Reactions and Equations.question: Which gas is flushed into packets of potato chips to prevent rancidity?
Chemical Reactions and Equations.explanation: Nitrogen is an unreactive inert gas that displaces oxygen, preventing the oxidation and foul odor/taste of oils and fats.

Chemical Reactions and Equations.question: Balancing a chemical equation is fundamentally based on which law of nature?
Chemical Reactions and Equations.explanation: Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction; hence total atoms of each element on reactant side must equal the product side.

Acids, Bases and Salts.question: Why does dry HCl gas not change the color of dry blue litmus paper?
options: HCl dissociates into H⁺ ions only in the presence of water/moisture
Dry litmus paper cannot absorb gas molecules
HCl is basic in gaseous form
Litmus paper only reacts with organic acids
Acids, Bases and Salts.correctAnswer: HCl dissociates into H⁺ ions only in the presence of water/moisture
Acids, Bases and Salts.conceptTag: Ionization of Acids in Aqueous Media
Acids, Bases and Salts.explanation: Acidic behavior is caused by hydronium (H₃O⁺) or H⁺ ions. In dry conditions, HCl molecules do not dissociate, exhibiting no acidic property.

Acids, Bases and Salts.question: What is the pH value of a completely neutral aqueous solution at 25°C?
Acids, Bases and Salts.explanation: At standard temperature, pure water has [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁷ M, resulting in pH 7.

Acids, Bases and Salts.question: Which gas is liberated when an active metal reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid?
Acids, Bases and Salts.explanation: Metal + Dilute Acid → Metal Salt + H₂ gas (which burns with a characteristic pop sound).

Acids, Bases and Salts.question: What happens when excess carbon dioxide is passed through limewater?
options: The milkiness disappears due to the formation of soluble Ca(HCO₃)₂
A thick black precipitate settles down
Acids, Bases and Salts.correctAnswer: The milkiness disappears due to the formation of soluble Ca(HCO₃)₂
Acids, Bases and Salts.conceptTag: Limewater Test and Excess CO₂ Effect
Acids, Bases and Salts.explanation: Initial milkiness is due to insoluble CaCO₃. Excess CO₂ converts it into soluble calcium hydrogen carbonate: CaCO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ → Ca(HCO₃)₂.

Acids, Bases and Salts.question: What is the chemical formula of Plaster of Paris?
Acids, Bases and Salts.explanation: Plaster of Paris is calcium sulphate hemihydrate (CaSO₄ · ½ H₂O), formed by heating gypsum (CaSO₄ · 2 H₂O) to 373 K.

Acids, Bases and Salts.question: Tooth decay starts when the pH in the oral cavity falls below:
Acids, Bases and Salts.explanation: Enamel (calcium hydroxyapatite) corrodes when bacteria degrade sugar residues, dropping mouth pH below 5.5.

Acids, Bases and Salts.question: Which of the following salts produces an acidic aqueous solution when dissolved in water?
Acids, Bases and Salts.conceptTag: Hydrolysis of Strong Acid - Weak Base Salts
Acids, Bases and Salts.explanation: NH₄Cl is formed from a strong acid (HCl) and a weak base (NH₄OH); its cation undergoes hydrolysis, yielding an acidic solution (pH < 7).

Acids, Bases and Salts.question: Why is adding water to concentrated acid strictly avoided, and instead acid is added to water with constant stirring?
options: Dilution is highly exothermic and can cause dangerous acid splashing
Acid will evaporate instantly without mixing
Water loses its density and freezes
Acids, Bases and Salts.correctAnswer: Dilution is highly exothermic and can cause dangerous acid splashing
Acids, Bases and Salts.conceptTag: Safety and Enthalpy of Acid Dilution
Acids, Bases and Salts.explanation: Adding water to concentrated acid releases sudden localized heat that can boil the water instantly and splatter corrosive acid onto the user.

Metals and Non-metals.question: Which metal is liquid at standard room temperature?
Metals and Non-metals.explanation: Mercury (Hg) is the only metallic element that remains liquid at room temperature (Bromine is a liquid non-metal).

Metals and Non-metals.question: Why are sodium and potassium stored under kerosene oil?
options: They react vigorously with moisture and oxygen in the air catching fire
They dissolve completely in atmospheric nitrogen
Kerosene enhances their metallic electrical conductivity
To prevent them from evaporating at ambient temperatures
Metals and Non-metals.correctAnswer: They react vigorously with moisture and oxygen in the air catching fire
Metals and Non-metals.explanation: Sodium and potassium react violently and exothermically with atmospheric O₂ and water vapor, producing flammable hydrogen gas.

Metals and Non-metals.question: Which non-metal is lustrous and has a shiny surface?
Metals and Non-metals.explanation: Although non-metals are typically dull, Iodine crystals possess a metallic purplish-grey luster.

Metals and Non-metals.question: What is an amphoteric oxide?
options: An oxide that reacts with both acids and bases to produce salt and water
An oxide that dissolves only in organic solvents
An oxide that has a neutral pH of 7
An oxide that turns blue litmus red only
Metals and Non-metals.correctAnswer: An oxide that reacts with both acids and bases to produce salt and water
Metals and Non-metals.explanation: Oxides like Al₂O₃ and ZnO react with both acids (behaving as a base) and strong alkalis (behaving as an acid) to form salt and water.

Metals and Non-metals.question: Which method is used to prevent the rusting of iron by coating it with a thin layer of zinc?
Metals and Non-metals.explanation: Galvanisation applies a sacrificial zinc layer over iron. Even if scratched, zinc oxidizes preferentially before iron.

Metals and Non-metals.question: What type of bond is formed when electrons are completely transferred from a metal atom to a non-metal atom?
Metals and Non-metals.explanation: Metals lose electrons to form positive cations, while non-metals gain them to form negative anions, held by electrostatic attraction.

Metals and Non-metals.question: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity in molten state or aqueous solution but NOT in solid state?
options: Ions are locked in rigid lattice positions in solid state but free to move in liquid state
Electrons disappear in solid ionic crystals
Solid salts do not have charged particles
Metals and Non-metals.correctAnswer: Ions are locked in rigid lattice positions in solid state but free to move in liquid state
Metals and Non-metals.explanation: Solid ionic compounds have strong electrostatic lattice forces keeping ions immobile. Molten state or hydration frees ions to carry charge.

Metals and Non-metals.question: What is an amalgam?
options: An alloy where one of the constituent metals is mercury
An alloy composed purely of non-metals
A compound of iron and carbon
Metals and Non-metals.correctAnswer: An alloy where one of the constituent metals is mercury
Metals and Non-metals.explanation: An amalgam is an alloy of mercury with one or more other metals (e.g., sodium amalgam, dental silver amalgam).

Carbon and its Compounds.question: Why does carbon form covalent bonds rather than ionic bonds (C⁴⁺ or C⁴⁻)?
options: Forming C⁴⁺ requires enormous energy to remove 4 electrons, and gaining 4 electrons makes holding 6 protons for 10 electrons unstable
Carbon is an inert noble gas
Carbon and its Compounds.correctAnswer: Forming C⁴⁺ requires enormous energy to remove 4 electrons, and gaining 4 electrons makes holding 6 protons for 10 electrons unstable
Carbon and its Compounds.explanation: With 4 valence electrons, carbon achieves stability by sharing pairs of electrons (covalent bonding) rather than full electron transfer.

Carbon and its Compounds.question: What is 'Catenation'?
options: The unique ability of carbon atoms to link with other carbon atoms to form long chains, branched chains, and rings
The property of carbon burning with a blue flame
The conversion of graphite into diamond at high pressure
The bonding of carbon with oxygen to form CO₂
Carbon and its Compounds.correctAnswer: The unique ability of carbon atoms to link with other carbon atoms to form long chains, branched chains, and rings
Carbon and its Compounds.explanation: Due to its small size and strong carbon-carbon covalent bond strength, carbon exhibits catenation to a far greater extent than any other element.

Carbon and its Compounds.question: What is the general formula of acyclic saturated hydrocarbons (Alkanes)?
Carbon and its Compounds.explanation: Alkanes contain only single carbon-carbon bonds and follow the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

Carbon and its Compounds.question: What is the structural difference between diamond and graphite, both of which are allotropes of carbon?
options: In diamond, each carbon is tetrahedrally bonded to 4 others forming a rigid 3D network; in graphite, carbons are bonded in hexagonal layers with weak Van der Waals forces allowing layers to slide
Diamond is made of pure silicon, while graphite is pure lead
Graphite is a 3D rigid crystal, while diamond is composed of 2D slippery sheets
Diamond conducts electricity while graphite is an electrical insulator
Carbon and its Compounds.correctAnswer: In diamond, each carbon is tetrahedrally bonded to 4 others forming a rigid 3D network; in graphite, carbons are bonded in hexagonal layers with weak Van der Waals forces allowing layers to slide
Carbon and its Compounds.explanation: Diamond's 3D covalent network makes it extremely hard; graphite's layered sheets with delocalized electrons make it soft, slippery, and a good electrical conductor.

Carbon and its Compounds.question: What functional group is present in Ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH)?
Carbon and its Compounds.explanation: The hydroxyl group (-OH) characterizes alcoholic organic compounds.

Carbon and its Compounds.question: What happens when ethanol is heated with excess concentrated sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) at 443 K?
options: Ethanol undergoes dehydration to form ethene gas (alkene)
Ethanol reacts with sodium to form carbon dioxide
Carbon and its Compounds.correctAnswer: Ethanol undergoes dehydration to form ethene gas (alkene)
Carbon and its Compounds.explanation: Concentrated H₂SO₄ acts as a dehydrating agent, removing a water molecule from ethanol to yield unsaturated ethene (CH₂=CH₂).

Carbon and its Compounds.question: How do soaps clean greasy clothes (Micelle formation)?
options: Soap molecules have a hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail that attaches to oil/grease and a hydrophilic ionic head that dissolves in water, forming spherical clusters called micelles that wash away
Soap dissolves grease by turning it into solid stone
Soap heats up the water to boil off grease
Carbon and its Compounds.correctAnswer: Soap molecules have a hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail that attaches to oil/grease and a hydrophilic ionic head that dissolves in water, forming spherical clusters called micelles that wash away
Carbon and its Compounds.explanation: The dual nature of soap molecules allows them to emulsify oily dirt into water-suspensible micelles during agitation.

Carbon and its Compounds.question: Why do soaps fail to lather in hard water containing dissolved calcium and magnesium salts, whereas synthetic detergents work effectively?
options: Soaps react with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions to form an insoluble sticky precipitate called scum, whereas synthetic detergents form soluble calcium and magnesium salts
Hard water destroys all detergent molecules permanently
Soaps turn into pure alcohol in hard water
Detergents contain acid that dissolves hard water minerals
Carbon and its Compounds.correctAnswer: Soaps react with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions to form an insoluble sticky precipitate called scum, whereas synthetic detergents form soluble calcium and magnesium salts
Carbon and its Compounds.conceptTag: Hard Water vs Soaps and Detergents
Carbon and its Compounds.explanation: Scum wastes soap and hinders cleaning in hard water; synthetic detergents bypass this because their charged sulphonate/sulphate heads do not precipitate with calcium or magnesium.

Life Processes.question: Where does the light-independent (dark) reaction or carbon fixation phase of photosynthesis take place in the chloroplast?
Life Processes.explanation: Light reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes (grana), while Calvin cycle enzymes are located in the liquid stroma.

Life Processes.question: What is the role of bile juice secreted by the liver in the human digestive system?
options: Emulsification of large fat globules and providing an alkaline medium
Digestion of proteins into amino acids
Life Processes.correctAnswer: Emulsification of large fat globules and providing an alkaline medium
Life Processes.explanation: Bile contains no digestive enzymes; it emulsifies fats into smaller micelles and creates the alkaline pH required for pancreatic lipase.

Life Processes.question: During anaerobic respiration in human muscle cells during vigorous exercise, pyruvate is converted into:
Life Processes.explanation: Due to insufficient oxygen, muscle cells reduce pyruvate into 3-carbon lactic acid, causing localized muscle cramps.

Life Processes.question: Why do ventricles have thicker muscular walls than atria in the human heart?
options: Ventricles have to pump blood with high pressure to distant organs
Atria store blood under high hydraulic pressure
Ventricles prevent backward flow of deoxygenated blood
Atria are directly connected to systemic capillary beds
Life Processes.correctAnswer: Ventricles have to pump blood with high pressure to distant organs
Life Processes.explanation: Atria only pump blood down into adjacent ventricles, whereas ventricles (especially the left) pump blood tolungs and entire body against resistance.

Life Processes.question: What is the structural and functional filtration unit of the human kidney?
Life Processes.explanation: Each human kidney contains roughly 1 million nephrons responsible for filtration, reabsorption, and urine excretion.

Life Processes.question: Which vascular tissue transports sucrose, amino acids, and hormones bidirectionally in vascular plants?
Life Processes.explanation: Xylem conducts water/minerals unidirectionally upward. Phloem moves photosynthates bidirectionally from source to sink via active translocation.

Life Processes.question: What prevents the collapse of the human trachea when there is less air inside it?
Life Processes.explanation: Incomplete cartilaginous rings maintain structural rigidity in the trachea, preventing mechanical collapse during inhalation.

Life Processes.question: What is the primary driving force for upward water movement in tall trees during daylight hours?
Life Processes.explanation: Evaporation of water from stomata creates a negative suction tension throughout the xylem vessel column, pulling water upward.

Control and Coordination.question: What is the junction or microscopic gap between two communicating neurons called?
Control and Coordination.explanation: The synapse is the functional contact point where electrical impulses trigger neurotransmitter release across the synaptic cleft.

Control and Coordination.question: Which plant hormone is primarily responsible for promoting cell elongation and phototropism?
Control and Coordination.explanation: Auxin accumulates on the shaded side of shoot tips, stimulating faster cell elongation and bending the shoot toward light.

Control and Coordination.question: Which part of the human brain controls involuntary vital functions like heartbeat, blood pressure, and salivation?
Control and Coordination.explanation: The medulla oblongata in the hindbrain houses cardiovascular, vasomotor, and swallowing/salivation reflex centers.

Control and Coordination.question: Which part of the brain is responsible for maintaining body posture, equilibrium, and precision of voluntary movements?
Control and Coordination.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates skeletal muscle contractions, ensuring precision, balance, and fine motor stability.

Control and Coordination.question: Which hormone promotes wilting, stomatal closure, and acts as a stress hormone in plants?
Control and Coordination.explanation: Abscisic acid inhibits growth, initiates stomatal closure under drought, and induces leaf/flower abscission.

Control and Coordination.question: Why is iodised salt recommended in dietary intake?
options: Iodine is essential for the thyroid gland to synthesize thyroxine
It prevents bacterial infection in salivary glands
It increases hemoglobin affinity for oxygen
It provides electrolytes for muscular contraction
Control and Coordination.correctAnswer: Iodine is essential for the thyroid gland to synthesize thyroxine
Control and Coordination.explanation: Thyroxine regulates carbohydrate, protein, and fat metabolism. Iodine deficiency impairs its synthesis, causing goitre.

Control and Coordination.question: In a reflex arc, where is the rapid integration between sensory and motor neurons processed?
Control and Coordination.explanation: Reflex actions bypass direct brain control to save critical response time, integrating through interneurons in the spinal cord.

Control and Coordination.question: Which endocrine gland secretes insulin to regulate blood glucose concentrations?
Control and Coordination.explanation: Beta cells of the Islets of Langerhans in the pancreas secrete insulin, promoting cellular uptake of blood glucose.

How do Organisms Reproduce?.question: What is the primary evolutionary advantage of sexual reproduction over asexual reproduction?
options: It generates genetic variation through DNA recombination, helping populations adapt to changing environments
It requires only a single parent and is much faster
It produces genetically identical clones every generation
It completely prevents all genetic mutations
How do Organisms Reproduce?.correctAnswer: It generates genetic variation through DNA recombination, helping populations adapt to changing environments
How do Organisms Reproduce?.explanation: Combining DNA from two parents via meiosis and fertilization introduces variations that enable species survival under environmental shifts.

How do Organisms Reproduce?.question: How does 'multiple fission' in Plasmodium (malaria parasite) differ from 'binary fission' in Amoeba?
options: In multiple fission, the parent nucleus divides repeatedly within a cyst to form many daughter cells simultaneously
In multiple fission, only two unequal buds are formed
Multiple fission only occurs in multicellular plants
How do Organisms Reproduce?.correctAnswer: In multiple fission, the parent nucleus divides repeatedly within a cyst to form many daughter cells simultaneously
How do Organisms Reproduce?.explanation: Amoeba splits into two cells by binary fission, whereas Plasmodium divides its nucleus multiple times inside a protective cyst before releasing dozens of daughter cells.

How do Organisms Reproduce?.question: Why do agriculturists prefer 'vegetative propagation' (such as grafting or layering) for cultivating seedless fruits like banana, rose, and jasmine?
options: It preserves desirable parental traits and enables propagation of plants that have lost the capacity to produce viable seeds
It introduces massive random genetic mutations
Plants grown by vegetative propagation take twice as long to bear flowers
How do Organisms Reproduce?.correctAnswer: It preserves desirable parental traits and enables propagation of plants that have lost the capacity to produce viable seeds
How do Organisms Reproduce?.explanation: Vegetative propagation produces genetically uniform plants that flower and fruit earlier than seed-grown plants and bypasses seed sterility.

How do Organisms Reproduce?.question: In a flowering plant (angiosperm), after fertilization, what do the 'ovule' and the 'ovary' develop into respectively?
options: Ovule develops into a tough-coated Seed; Ovary ripens into a Fruit
Ovule develops into a Fruit; Ovary develops into a Seed
Both shrivel and fall off the plant
Ovule becomes the petal; Ovary becomes the sepal
How do Organisms Reproduce?.correctAnswer: Ovule develops into a tough-coated Seed; Ovary ripens into a Fruit
How do Organisms Reproduce?.explanation: Following fertilization, the zygote inside the ovule forms the embryo, the ovule becomes the seed, and the surrounding ovary swells into the fruit.

How do Organisms Reproduce?.question: Where does fertilization typically occur in the human female reproductive system?
How do Organisms Reproduce?.explanation: Sperm meets and fertilizes the ovum inside the ampulla of the fallopian tube before the zygote implants into the uterine lining.

How do Organisms Reproduce?.question: What is the function of the prostate gland and seminal vesicles in the human male reproductive system?
options: To secrete fluid that provides nourishment to sperms and facilitates their transport
How do Organisms Reproduce?.correctAnswer: To secrete fluid that provides nourishment to sperms and facilitates their transport
How do Organisms Reproduce?.explanation: Seminal vesicles and prostate gland add seminal plasma secretions that nourish sperm and provide a fluid medium for motility.

How do Organisms Reproduce?.question: Which of the following is a barrier method of contraception that also provides protection against sexually transmitted diseases (STDs)?
How do Organisms Reproduce?.explanation: Barrier methods like condoms physically prevent sperm-egg contact and reduce infection transmission, unlike pills or IUDs.

How do Organisms Reproduce?.question: What is the surgical method of contraception performed in human females by blocking the fallopian tubes?
How do Organisms Reproduce?.explanation: Tubectomy blocks fallopian tubes in females to prevent eggs from reaching the uterus; vasectomy blocks vas deferens in males.

Heredity.question: What is Mendel's 'Law of Segregation' (First Law)?
options: Alleles separate during gamete formation so that each gamete carries only one allele for each gene
Genes for different traits are inherited independently of each other
Dominant traits completely mask recessive traits in every generation
Acquired characters are passed on to offspring
Heredity.correctAnswer: Alleles separate during gamete formation so that each gamete carries only one allele for each gene
Heredity.explanation: During meiosis, paired alleles segregate randomly so that each gamete receives a single allele per locus.

Heredity.question: In Mendel's monohybrid cross of tall (TT) and dwarf (tt) pea plants, what is the phenotypic ratio observed in the F₂ generation?
Heredity.explanation: The F₂ generation yields 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt genotypically, which translates to a 3:1 phenotypic ratio of tall to dwarf plants.

Heredity.question: What is the phenotypic ratio in a Mendel's dihybrid cross involving two independent traits in the F₂ generation?
Heredity.explanation: A dihybrid cross (e.g., round-yellow x wrinkled-green) yields 9 round-yellow, 3 round-green, 3 wrinkled-yellow, and 1 wrinkled-green (9:3:3:1).

Heredity.question: How is the sex of a child determined genetically in human beings?
options: By whether the sperm carries an X or a Y chromosome to fertilize the X-bearing egg
By the temperature of the external environment during embryonic development
By whether the mother contributes a Y chromosome
Heredity.correctAnswer: By whether the sperm carries an X or a Y chromosome to fertilize the X-bearing egg
Heredity.explanation: Human females are homogametic (XX) producing only X eggs; males are heterogametic (XY) producing X and Y sperm, determining offspring sex.

Heredity.question: What is the difference between an organism's 'genotype' and its 'phenotype'?
options: Genotype is the genetic constitution (allele combination), whereas phenotype is the observable physical or biochemical trait
Genotype is visible to the eye, while phenotype is hidden inside DNA
Genotype changes with age, while phenotype never changes
Genotype applies only to plants, phenotype to animals
Heredity.correctAnswer: Genotype is the genetic constitution (allele combination), whereas phenotype is the observable physical or biochemical trait
Heredity.explanation: Genotype represents the underlying gene alleles (e.g., Tt), while phenotype represents the expressed physical trait (e.g., Tall).

Heredity.question: Why are acquired traits (like muscle mass built by rigorous exercise or loss of a finger in an accident) not inherited by offspring?
options: They do not cause any change in the DNA of germ cells (sperms/eggs)
Acquired traits are immediately deleted by enzymes in the zygote
Only dominant genes can be acquired
Heredity.correctAnswer: They do not cause any change in the DNA of germ cells (sperms/eggs)
Heredity.explanation: Changes occurring in somatic (body) tissues are not transmitted to progeny; only germline genetic modifications affect inheritance.

Heredity.question: What is 'genetic drift'?
options: A random change in allele frequencies in a population from generation to generation due to chance events
The migration of animals to a new forest
The targeted selection of fast runners by predators
The intentional cross-breeding of crops by farmers
Heredity.correctAnswer: A random change in allele frequencies in a population from generation to generation due to chance events
Heredity.explanation: Genetic drift is an evolutionary mechanism driven by random sampling error, highly pronounced in small populations (bottleneck/founder effects).

Heredity.question: What are 'homologous organs' (e.g., forelimbs of humans, lizards, birds, and whales)?
options: Organs that have the same fundamental structural/embryonic origin but perform different functions
Organs that look identical and perform identical functions but have different evolutionary origins
Organs that have shrunk and lost all biological function
Organs found only in fossilized reptiles
Heredity.correctAnswer: Organs that have the same fundamental structural/embryonic origin but perform different functions
Heredity.explanation: Homologous structures indicate common ancestry (divergent evolution), whereas analogous organs (like bird and insect wings) indicate convergent evolution.

Light – Reflection and Refraction.question: What is the relationship between the focal length f and radius of curvature R for a spherical mirror of small aperture?
Light – Reflection and Refraction.explanation: For paraxial rays striking a spherical mirror of small aperture, the principal focus lies halfway between pole and center of curvature: f = R / 2.

Light – Reflection and Refraction.question: Where should an object be placed in front of a concave mirror to obtain a virtual, erect, and magnified image?
options: Between the pole (P) and principal focus (F)
Light – Reflection and Refraction.correctAnswer: Between the pole (P) and principal focus (F)
Light – Reflection and Refraction.conceptTag: Virtual Image Ray Optics for Concave Mirror
Light – Reflection and Refraction.explanation: When an object is placed between P and F of a concave mirror, the reflected rays diverge and appear to intersect behind the mirror.

Light – Reflection and Refraction.question: Why are convex mirrors preferred as rear-view mirrors in automobiles?
options: They always form erect, diminished images giving a wider field of view
Light – Reflection and Refraction.correctAnswer: They always form erect, diminished images giving a wider field of view
Light – Reflection and Refraction.conceptTag: Convex Mirror Field of View Application
Light – Reflection and Refraction.explanation: Convex mirrors curve outward, creating upright diminished images and giving drivers a much wider viewing perspective.

Light – Reflection and Refraction.question: What is the SI unit of the optical power of a lens?
Light – Reflection and Refraction.explanation: Power is defined as P = 1 / f(in metres). The SI unit of lens power is the dioptre (m⁻¹).

Light – Reflection and Refraction.question: When a ray of light enters an optically denser medium from an optically rarer medium at an angle, it:
options: Bends toward the normal and its speed decreases
Bends away from the normal and its speed increases
Light – Reflection and Refraction.correctAnswer: Bends toward the normal and its speed decreases
Light – Reflection and Refraction.conceptTag: Snell's Law and Refractive Speed Changes
Light – Reflection and Refraction.explanation: In an optically denser medium, speed of light decreases. By Snell's Law (n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r), the ray refracts toward the normal.

Light – Reflection and Refraction.question: What is the refractive index of a medium if the speed of light in it is 2 × 10⁸ m/s (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)?
A convex lens produces a real and inverted image of the same size as the object when the object is placed at:
Light – Reflection and Refraction.explanation: Placing an object at 2F₁ yields an image at 2F₂ with magnification m = -1 (real, inverted, equal size).

Light – Reflection and Refraction.question: What is the magnification formula for spherical lenses in terms of image distance v and object distance u?
Light – Reflection and Refraction.conceptTag: Lens vs Mirror Magnification Sign Convention
Light – Reflection and Refraction.explanation: For lenses, magnification m = v / u (positive ratio). For spherical mirrors, m = -v / u.

The Human Eye and the Colourful World.question: What is the function of the ciliary muscles in the human eye?
options: To modify the curvature of the crystalline lens, enabling 'accommodation' for focusing on near and distant objects
To control the total amount of light entering the pupil
To convert light rays into electrical nerve impulses
To maintain the shape of the eyeball by secreting vitreous humor
The Human Eye and the Colourful World.correctAnswer: To modify the curvature of the crystalline lens, enabling 'accommodation' for focusing on near and distant objects
The Human Eye and the Colourful World.explanation: Ciliary muscles relax to flatten the lens for distant vision and contract to thicken the lens for near focusing.

The Human Eye and the Colourful World.question: What is 'Myopia' (Near-sightedness), and how is it corrected?
options: A person can see nearby objects clearly but cannot see distant objects distinctly; corrected using a concave lens
A person can see distant objects clearly but not nearby objects; corrected using a convex lens
Loss of accommodation power in old age; corrected using bifocals
Uneven corneal curvature causing blurred vision; corrected using cylindrical lenses
The Human Eye and the Colourful World.correctAnswer: A person can see nearby objects clearly but cannot see distant objects distinctly; corrected using a concave lens
The Human Eye and the Colourful World.explanation: In myopia, distant images form in front of the retina; a diverging concave lens diverges incoming rays so they focus precisely on the retina.

The Human Eye and the Colourful World.question: Why does the clear sky appear blue during daytime?
options: Rayleigh scattering: shorter blue wavelengths of sunlight are scattered much more strongly by atmospheric air molecules than longer red wavelengths
Air molecules absorb all colors except blue and reflect it downward
The oceans reflect their blue color onto the upper atmosphere
Nitrogen gas in the air emits blue fluorescence when struck by sunlight
The Human Eye and the Colourful World.correctAnswer: Rayleigh scattering: shorter blue wavelengths of sunlight are scattered much more strongly by atmospheric air molecules than longer red wavelengths
The Human Eye and the Colourful World.explanation: Scattering intensity is inversely proportional to the fourth power of wavelength (I ∝ 1/λ⁴), making blue light scatter ~9.4 times more than red light.

The Human Eye and the Colourful World.question: Why do the Sun and surrounding sky appear reddish during sunrise and sunset?
options: Light travels through a much thicker layer of atmosphere at the horizon, scattering away most blue and shorter wavelengths, leaving mostly red and orange wavelengths to reach our eyes
The Sun changes its chemical composition and turns into a red giant every evening
Sunset temperatures make the air red
Carbon dioxide levels spike during evening hours
The Human Eye and the Colourful World.correctAnswer: Light travels through a much thicker layer of atmosphere at the horizon, scattering away most blue and shorter wavelengths, leaving mostly red and orange wavelengths to reach our eyes
The Human Eye and the Colourful World.conceptTag: Reddish Appearance of Sun at Sunrise/Sunset
The Human Eye and the Colourful World.explanation: At the horizon, light path length is maximized, scattering away shorter wavelengths and transmitting only least-scattered longer red wavelengths.

The Human Eye and the Colourful World.question: What causes the phenomenon of a 'Rainbow' in the sky after a rain shower?
options: Dispersion, total internal reflection, and refraction of sunlight through tiny spherical water droplets acting as prisms
Reflection of light off flat clouds like mirrors
Electrical discharge between raindrops and lightning
Diffraction of light through dry dust particles
The Human Eye and the Colourful World.explanation: Water droplets refract, disperse white sunlight into constituent colors, internally reflect off the back surface, and refract again upon exiting toward the observer.

The Human Eye and the Colourful World.question: What is 'Hypermetropia' (Far-sightedness), and how is it corrected?
options: A person can see distant objects clearly but nearby objects appear blurred; corrected using a convex lens
Inability to distinguish between red and green colors
Clouding of the crystalline lens causing blindness
Inability of the pupil to dilate in darkness
The Human Eye and the Colourful World.correctAnswer: A person can see distant objects clearly but nearby objects appear blurred; corrected using a convex lens
The Human Eye and the Colourful World.explanation: In hypermetropia, images of near objects focus behind the retina; a converging convex lens adds converging power to focus light on the retina.

The Human Eye and the Colourful World.question: Why do stars appear to 'twinkle' at night, whereas planets do not?
options: Stars are distant point-sized sources of light whose rays undergo rapid atmospheric refraction through fluctuating air layers; planets are extended sources (collections of point sources) whose variations average out to zero
Stars switch their nuclear fusion reactors on and off every second
Planets produce their own stable laser light
Earth's magnetic field blocks starlight periodically
The Human Eye and the Colourful World.correctAnswer: Stars are distant point-sized sources of light whose rays undergo rapid atmospheric refraction through fluctuating air layers; planets are extended sources (collections of point sources) whose variations average out to zero
The Human Eye and the Colourful World.conceptTag: Atmospheric Twinkling of Stars vs Planets
The Human Eye and the Colourful World.explanation: Starlight flickers due to atmospheric density fluctuations bending light path randomly; planet discs average out these fluctuations, appearing steady.

The Human Eye and the Colourful World.question: What is 'Presbyopia', and what is the typical corrective eyewear prescribed for it?
options: Gradual weakening of ciliary muscles and loss of lens flexibility with age; corrected using bifocal lenses (containing both concave and convex parts)
Total color blindness treated with dark glasses
Permanent dilation of pupils treated with eye drops
Complete opacification of the cornea treated with transplants
The Human Eye and the Colourful World.correctAnswer: Gradual weakening of ciliary muscles and loss of lens flexibility with age; corrected using bifocal lenses (containing both concave and convex parts)
The Human Eye and the Colourful World.explanation: As people age, accommodation power declines (presbyopia), often requiring bifocals to see both distant and near objects clearly.

Electricity.question: Ohm's Law states that the current I flowing through a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference V across its ends, provided:
options: Temperature and other physical conditions remain constant
The circuit is kept under zero atmospheric pressure
The magnetic field is strictly zero
Electricity.correctAnswer: Temperature and other physical conditions remain constant
Electricity.explanation: Ohm's Law (V = IR) holds true only if temperature and dimensions remain unchanged, because resistance varies with temperature.

Electricity.question: If the length of a uniform cylindrical metallic wire is doubled by stretching, what happens to its resistance?
Electricity.explanation: Volume V = A * L remains constant. Doubling length (L' = 2L) halves cross-sectional area (A' = A/2). New R' = ρ(2L)/(A/2) = 4 * (ρL/A) = 4R.

Electricity.question: What is the equivalent resistance of three identical resistors of resistance R connected in parallel?
According to Joule's Law of Heating, the heat H produced in a resistor of resistance R carrying current I for time t is:
Electricity.explanation: Electrical work W = VIt = (IR)It = I²Rt. This energy dissipates as heat H = I²Rt.

Electricity.question: What is the commercial unit of electrical energy (1 kilowatt-hour, kWh) in Joules?
Why is an ammeter always connected in series in an electric circuit?
options: It has very low internal resistance to ensure the whole circuit current passes through it without voltage drop
It has infinite resistance to block high currents
It measures potential differences across branches
It acts as a safety fuse
Electricity.correctAnswer: It has very low internal resistance to ensure the whole circuit current passes through it without voltage drop
Electricity.explanation: An ideal ammeter has zero internal resistance, ensuring it does not alter total circuit current when wired in series.

Electricity.question: Why is tungsten metal used almost exclusively for the filament of incandescent electric lamps?
options: It has a very high melting point and high resistivity, glowing white without melting
It is the best conductor of electricity among all metals
It oxidizes easily at low temperatures
It is cheap and soft like copper
Electricity.correctAnswer: It has a very high melting point and high resistivity, glowing white without melting
Electricity.explanation: Tungsten has an exceptionally high melting point (3380°C) and emits visible incandescence when heated.

Electricity.question: What happens to the electrical resistivity of a metallic wire if its length and radius are doubled?
Electricity.explanation: Resistivity (ρ) is an intrinsic material property that depends only on the nature of the material and temperature, not dimensions.

Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.question: What is the shape of magnetic field lines around a straight current-carrying wire?
options: Concentric circles centered on the wire
Straight parallel lines pointing away from the wire
Elliptical loops along the length of wire
Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.correctAnswer: Concentric circles centered on the wire
Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.explanation: By Maxwell's Right-Hand Thumb Rule, circular concentric magnetic lines surround any straight conductor carrying electric current.

Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.question: Inside a long current-carrying cylindrical solenoid, the magnetic field is:
options: Uniform and parallel to the axis
Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.correctAnswer: Uniform and parallel to the axis
Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.explanation: The field lines inside a solenoid run parallel and equidistant along the axis, indicating a uniform magnetic field.

Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.question: Which rule gives the direction of magnetic force experienced by a current-carrying conductor in an external magnetic field?
Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.explanation: Fleming's Left-Hand Rule determines mechanical force/motion direction (Thumb) using Magnetic Field (Forefinger) and Current (Middle finger).

Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.question: Why do two magnetic field lines never intersect each other?
options: At the point of intersection, a compass needle would have to point in two different directions simultaneously, which is impossible
Magnetic lines repel each other by electrostatic force
Lines only exist inside magnetic materials
Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.correctAnswer: At the point of intersection, a compass needle would have to point in two different directions simultaneously, which is impossible
Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.explanation: The tangent to a field line gives the unique resultant magnetic field vector direction. Intersecting lines would imply two simultaneous resultant directions at one point.

Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.question: What is the function of the earth wire in domestic electric circuits?
options: It provides a low-resistance path to direct accidental leakage currents safely to the ground
It completes the AC live circuit loop
Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.correctAnswer: It provides a low-resistance path to direct accidental leakage currents safely to the ground
Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.explanation: The earth wire connects metal appliances to the ground, preventing electric shocks by tripping the circuit if live wires contact metal casings.

Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.question: What type of current is supplied to domestic households in India, and at what frequency?
Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.explanation: Standard domestic electrical supply in India operates at 220 V Alternating Current with a frequency of 50 Hz (100 reversals per second).

Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.question: What is an electromagnet?
options: A soft iron core placed inside a current-carrying solenoid
A piece of permanently magnetized steel
A copper bar wrapped in insulation without current
An aluminium plate exposed to sunlight
Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.correctAnswer: A soft iron core placed inside a current-carrying solenoid
Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.explanation: Soft iron has high magnetic permeability and loses its magnetism as soon as current stops, making it ideal for temporary electromagnets.

Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.question: What is the phenomenon of generating an electric current in a circuit by changing the magnetic flux linked with it?
Magnetic Effects of Electric Current.explanation: Discovered by Michael Faraday, electromagnetic induction produces an induced EMF/current across a conductor when exposed to varying magnetic flux.

Our Environment.question: Why is the flow of energy in a food chain always unidirectional and non-cyclic?
options: Energy captured by autotrophs is progressively dissipated as heat across trophic levels and cannot be recycled back to the sun
Energy increases as it moves up higher trophic levels
Decomposers convert heat back into solar radiation
Carnivores consume 100% of the energy from herbivores
Our Environment.correctAnswer: Energy captured by autotrophs is progressively dissipated as heat across trophic levels and cannot be recycled back to the sun
Our Environment.explanation: By the laws of thermodynamics, energy degrades into unusable heat at every trophic transfer, preventing energy cycling.

Our Environment.question: What is 'Biological Magnification' (Biomagnification)?
options: The progressive increase in concentration of non-biodegradable toxic chemicals (like DDT or heavy metals) at successive trophic levels
The multiplication of animal populations in a forest
The increase in plant height due to fertilizers
Our Environment.correctAnswer: The progressive increase in concentration of non-biodegradable toxic chemicals (like DDT or heavy metals) at successive trophic levels
Our Environment.explanation: Since non-biodegradable pollutants cannot be metabolized, their tissue concentrations multiply drastically as predators consume multiple contaminated prey.

Our Environment.question: How is stratospheric ozone formed, and why is its depletion by chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) dangerous?
options: Ozone forms when UV radiation splits O₂ molecules into free oxygen atoms that combine with O₂; CFCs release chlorine atoms that catalytically destroy ozone molecules, letting harmful UV-B radiation reach Earth
Ozone is formed by burning coal, and its loss causes global cooling
CFCs turn ozone into breathable oxygen gas, which is beneficial
Ozone depletion causes earthquakes and volcanic eruptions
Our Environment.correctAnswer: Ozone forms when UV radiation splits O₂ molecules into free oxygen atoms that combine with O₂; CFCs release chlorine atoms that catalytically destroy ozone molecules, letting harmful UV-B radiation reach Earth
Our Environment.explanation: Stratospheric ozone shields Earth from mutagenic UV radiation; free chlorine radicals from CFCs break down thousands of ozone molecules without being consumed.

Our Environment.question: What is the difference between biodegradable and non-biodegradable wastes?
options: Biodegradable wastes are broken down into harmless substances by biological action of microbes; non-biodegradable wastes cannot be decomposed and persist in the environment for centuries
Biodegradable wastes are made of synthetic plastic
Both types of waste decompose at the exact same rate
Our Environment.correctAnswer: Biodegradable wastes are broken down into harmless substances by biological action of microbes; non-biodegradable wastes cannot be decomposed and persist in the environment for centuries
Our Environment.explanation: Microbial saprophytes possess enzymes specific to organic matter, leaving synthetic polymers (plastics, glass) untouched.

Our Environment.question: According to the 10% Law, if plants in a grassland fix 10,000 kJ of energy, how much energy is available to tertiary carnivores (4th trophic level)?
Our Environment.explanation: Trophic level 1 (Producers): 10,000 kJ -> T1 to T2 (Herbivores): 1,000 kJ -> T2 to T3 (Carnivores): 100 kJ -> T3 to T4 (Tertiary): 10 kJ.

Our Environment.question: Which international agreement successfully restricted and phased out the production of ozone-depleting CFCs worldwide?
Our Environment.explanation: The Montreal Protocol stands as a landmark global treaty that successfully curbed ozone-depleting substances.

Our Environment.question: Why are food webs more stable and realistic representations of ecosystems than a simple linear food chain?
options: Real organisms eat multiple types of food and belong to multiple trophic levels, so if one prey species declines, predators can switch to alternative sources
Linear food chains always contain infinite species
Food webs do not include energy loss
Food webs only exist in aquatic environments
Our Environment.correctAnswer: Real organisms eat multiple types of food and belong to multiple trophic levels, so if one prey species declines, predators can switch to alternative sources
Our Environment.conceptTag: Food Web Complexity and Ecosystem Stability
Our Environment.explanation: Interconnected feeding relationships provide ecological resilience against population crashes or environmental shocks.

Our Environment.question: What is the role of decomposers (bacteria and fungi) in an ecosystem?
options: They break down complex organic wastes from dead plants and animals into simple inorganic nutrients, recycling matter back into the soil
They consume primary producers directly to generate solar energy
They remove all moisture from the atmosphere
Our Environment.correctAnswer: They break down complex organic wastes from dead plants and animals into simple inorganic nutrients, recycling matter back into the soil
Our Environment.conceptTag: Role of Decomposers in Nutrient Cycling
Our Environment.explanation: Decomposers act as nature's scavengers and recyclers, ensuring that vital chemical elements do not remain locked up in dead matter.
